---
title: "Simulation study: do the weights recover known effects?"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, out.width = "100%")
res <- read.csv("simulation-results.csv", check.names = FALSE)
se <- read.csv("simulation-se.csv", check.names = FALSE)
show <- function(prefix) {
  tab <- res[startsWith(res$scenario, prefix), c("method", "truth", "mean", "bias", "emp.sd", "rmse", "reps")]
  knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Method", "Truth", "Mean estimate", "Bias", "Empirical SD", "RMSE", "Replications"))
}
```

The new weights in ipw recover known causal effects when their model is
correct, and the naive or misspecified alternatives are clearly biased. This
article shows that with a simulation study in the spirit of the simulated
example in the JSS paper (van der Wal & Geskus 2011): each scenario
generates data in which the true marginal causal effect is known, estimates
it, and repeats this many times.

**How the results were produced.** The study is in
[`dev/simulation-study.R`](https://github.com/TranHung93/ipw/blob/main/dev/simulation-study.R)
in the repository; the code below shows the essential lines of each
scenario. It takes several minutes, so this page shows saved results rather
than running it. To reproduce them, run `Rscript dev/simulation-study.R` in the
package folder (seed 20261101), or start the `simulations` workflow from the
GitHub Actions tab. Scenarios 1 to 4 use 500 replications, 5 and 6 use 250,
and 7 uses 100 with 200 bootstrap samples each.

**Reading the tables.** *Bias* is the mean estimate minus the truth;
*empirical SD* is the spread of the estimates over replications; *RMSE*
combines both. A good method has bias close to 0 and a small RMSE.

```{r bias-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 7.5}
d <- res[!grepl("median", res$method), ]
d <- d[rev(seq_len(nrow(d))), ]
lab <- paste0(sub("\\..*", "", d$scenario), ". ", d$method)
good <- grepl("correct|ATE weights|ATT weights|ATO weights|ipwprob|s\\(l\\)|Cox|multinomial", d$method) &
  !grepl("misspecified", d$method)
cap <- 1
op <- par(mar = c(4, 20, 1, 1))
plot(pmin(d$bias, cap), seq_along(lab), pch = ifelse(good, 19, 1), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     xlab = "Bias (mean estimate minus truth)", xlim = c(-0.3, cap + 0.15))
axis(2, at = seq_along(lab), labels = lab, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.75)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
off <- d$bias > cap
text(rep(cap, sum(off)), which(off), sprintf("%.2f >", d$bias[off]), pos = 4, cex = 0.7)
legend("bottomright", pch = c(19, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       legend = c("new weights, correct model", "naive, misspecified or truncated"))
par(op)
```

# 1. ATE, ATT and overlap weights, and `ipwprob()`

The effect of a binary exposure varies with the confounder `l`, so the three
estimands differ. Their true values, computed from 2 million simulated
people, are ATE = 1, ATT = 1.276 and ATO = 0.861. Each weighting scheme is
compared with its own target; `ipwprob()` is given the true propensity
scores.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$a <- rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * d$l))
d$y <- d$a * (1 + d$l) + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = d, estimand = "ATT")$ipw.weights
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w.att))["a"]
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("1.")
```

All weighted estimates are unbiased for their own estimand; the unweighted
difference is nearly twice the ATE.

# 2. Count exposure: Poisson or negative binomial

The exposure is an overdispersed count (negative binomial, variance larger
than the mean); each extra unit raises the outcome by 0.5.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$v <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$v + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = v, family = "negbin", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("2.")
```

The negative binomial weights are unbiased. The Poisson model ignores the
overdispersion, and its weights over-correct: the bias is as large as that
of the unweighted analysis, in the other direction.

# 3. Skewed continuous exposure: gaussian, gamma or log-normal

The dose is log-normal given `l`; one unit of dose raises the outcome by 1.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(2000))
d$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * d$l + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))
d$y <- d$dose + 2 * d$l + rnorm(2000)
w.ln <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "lognormal", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("3.")
```

The log-normal weights remove most of the confounding, with a small
remaining bias (0.06) that is typical of weights for continuous exposures:
the density ratio has a heavy tail. The gaussian model is clearly biased, and
in 9 of 500 replications gave infinite weights, which `ipwpoint()` refuses.
The gamma model happens to have little bias here but twice the spread.
Truncation at the 1st and 99th percentiles reduces the spread a lot but adds
bias: the usual trade-off.

# 4. Curved propensity: smooth terms with mgcv

The probability of exposure depends on `l` through a sine curve; the true
effect is 2.

```{r eval = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
d$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * d$l)))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * d$l) + rnorm(2000)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = d)$ipw.weights
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("4.")
```

A straight-line logistic model leaves about a quarter of the confounding
bias in place; `s(l)` lets mgcv estimate the curve and removes almost all of it.

# 5. Time-varying ordinal dose, `type = "all"`

A dose level (0, 1, 2) is chosen at each of 4 visits from a proportional-odds
model given the confounder `L` and the previous dose. `L` is affected by the
previous dose and by an unmeasured `U`, which also affects the outcome. The
outcome rises by 1 per unit of cumulative dose. This is the situation in the
JSS paper where ordinary adjustment fails: `L` is both a confounder and
affected by earlier treatment.

```{r eval = FALSE}
for (t in 1:4) {
  l <- U + 0.4 * prev + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  dose <- findInterval(0.8 * l + 0.6 * prev + rlogis(n), c(0, 1.5))   # 0, 1, 2
  prev <- dose
}
y <- 1 * cumulative.dose + 2 * U + rnorm(n)

w <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
           numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
           id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
# weight at the last visit, then lm(y ~ cumulative.dose, weights = ...)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("5.")
```

The unweighted analysis is confounded, and adjusting for `L` at every visit
is biased in the other direction, because it blocks part of the effect and
opens a path through `U`. Both ordinal weights (the correct model) and
multinomial weights recover the effect.

# 6. Recurrent exposure events, `family = "survival"`, `type = "all"`

Exposure events (for example new prescriptions) happen repeatedly with a
known proportional hazard: baseline 2 per unit time, log hazard ratio 0.5 for
a fixed covariate `x` and -1 for a time-varying covariate `xt`. Because the
true hazard is known, the true weights are known too, so the check is on the
Cox coefficients and on how close the estimated weights are to the true ones.
In 6a all people share a grid of 10 intervals (as in `haartdat`); in 6b the
events happen in continuous time, `xt` changes at different times for each
person, and each event ends an interval (start-stop data cut at events, as in
Graffeo et al. 2018).

```{r eval = FALSE}
w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", denominator = ~ x + xt,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
coef(w$den.mod)
median(abs(log(w$ipw.weights / true.weights)))
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
show("6")
```

The Cox coefficients are unbiased in both designs, and the estimated
weights are typically within 7 to 9% of the true weights, which is the
estimation noise of the baseline hazard.

# 7. Standard errors: `ipwboot()` versus robust standard errors

The marginal structural model for a binary exposure (true effect 10,
n = 500) is fitted with stabilized weights; 95% confidence intervals come
from `ipwboot()` (200 bootstrap samples, re-estimating the weights) or from
robust standard errors (`survey::svyglm`). In 7a, exposure probabilities are
mostly between 0.1 and 0.9 (good overlap); 7b is the simulated example of the
JSS paper, where the logit of the propensity has a standard deviation of 5,
so many people are almost certain to be exposed or unexposed.

```{r eval = FALSE}
msm.effect <- function(dd) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = dd)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = dd, weights = w))["a"]
}
ipwboot(d, msm.effect, R = 200)
```

```{r echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(se, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Scenario", "Method", "Mean estimate", "Mean SE", "Empirical SD",
                           "Coverage of 95% CI", "Replications"))
```

With good overlap, both intervals reach their nominal 95% coverage; the
robust standard error is about 18% larger than the true spread of the
estimates and the bootstrap about 8%, in line with Austin (2016). In the JSS
example, the estimate itself is biased at this sample size (11.3 instead of
10) and both standard errors are far too small, so coverage is only about
50%. Near-violations of positivity, not the choice of standard error, are the
problem there: check the weights (`summary()`, `ipwplot()`) and consider
overlap weights or truncation.

# References

* Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of
  treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. *Statistics in
  Medicine* 35, 5642-5655.
* Graffeo N, Latouche A, Geskus RB, Chevret S (2018). Modeling time-varying
  exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. *Biometrical
  Journal* 60, 323-332.
* Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity
  score weighting. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 113,
  390-400.
* van der Wal WM, Geskus RB (2011). ipw: An R package for inverse probability
  weighting. *Journal of Statistical Software* 43(13), 1-23.
